Paper_name: Self-prioritization effect in the attentional blink paradigm: Attention-based or familiarity-based effect?
Summary: This study investigated the self-prioritization effect (SPE) using an attentional blink (AB) paradigm. In Experiment 1, shapes associated with 'you' (self), 'friend', or 'stranger' were used as the first target (T1). The AB effect was largest for the self-associated shape, followed by the friend-associated shape, suggesting self-associated stimuli have greater perceptual salience and attentional capture. In Experiment 2, participants underwent training to increase familiarity with all shape-label associations before the AB task. The performance difference between friend and stranger conditions disappeared, indicating the initial difference was due to familiarity. However, the advantage for the self-condition remained, supporting the SPE as a genuine effect beyond mere familiarity.
Author: Víctor Martínez-Pérez, Alejandro Sandoval-Lentisco, Miriam Tortajada, Lucía B. Palmero, Guillermo Campoy, Luis J. Fuentes
Conclusion: The self-prioritization effect (SPE) in the attentional blink paradigm is a genuine phenomenon not solely attributable to familiarity. While initial differences between friend and stranger conditions were driven by familiarity, the persistent advantage for self-associated stimuli, even after equalizing familiarity through training, indicates a unique attentional capture or perceptual salience linked to self-relevance.
